key_findings.finding: Secondary amenorrhea is generally defined as absence of menses for at least 3 months in someone with previously regular cycles (or about 6 months when cycles were previously irregular). At 2 months after stopping oral contraception, this patient does not yet meet the usual definition, so short-term observation is reasonable if pregnancy and concerning symptoms are absent.

source_tools.relevance: The retrieved guideline is the 2024 ASRM committee opinion specifically addressing definitions and diagnostic evaluation of primary and secondary amenorrhea, although its PubMed abstract does not display the full algorithm.

key_findings.finding: The recommended initial evaluation of established secondary amenorrhea begins by excluding pregnancy, followed by targeted endocrine testing—typically TSH and prolactin, with FSH (often interpreted with estradiol) to assess ovarian versus hypothalamic/pituitary causes. A serum beta-hCG is reasonable despite negative urine tests when amenorrhea is being formally evaluated, because urine testing can be falsely negative early or with dilute urine.

source_tools.relevance: The 2024 ASRM practice committee opinion is the most directly relevant guideline identified for diagnostic evaluation; the available abstract confirms its scope but not individual test recommendations.

key_findings.finding: FSH/estradiol, pelvic ultrasound, and a progesterone-withdrawal challenge are not all mandatory immediately in this low-risk 2-month post-pill scenario. FSH/estradiol and ultrasound are appropriate if amenorrhea persists to 3 months, initial TSH/prolactin or examination is abnormal, PCOS/ovarian insufficiency is suspected, or fertility evaluation is desired. Progesterone challenge is a secondary diagnostic maneuver rather than the preferred first test set and is not needed simply because menses has not returned after 2 months.

source_tools.relevance: The identified ASRM guideline is directly about the diagnostic strategy for amenorrhea; the search did not retrieve full-text algorithmic details, so this conclusion should be treated as guideline-consistent clinical synthesis rather than a directly quoted passage.

key_findings.finding: For this specific patient, a practical next step is either observation until 3 months from the last withdrawal bleed with follow-up, or—if clinician/patient prefers immediate evaluation—serum beta-hCG plus TSH and prolactin. If amenorrhea reaches 3 months or abnormalities emerge, add FSH/estradiol and consider pelvic ultrasound; investigate androgen excess/PCOS if acne becomes clinically significant or other hyperandrogenic features develop.
